Abstract
This paper presents data from large, isolated n-dodecane droplets burning in microgravity on the International Space Station, along with preliminary comparisons with numerical and analytic predictions indicating general agreement in trends. The tests involved were primarily in air (a few in reduced oxygen) at ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. After ignition, the droplets burn with a hot flame that extinguishes when the radiant energy loss causes the flame temperature to drop below the hot-flame-required value. The total flame radiative loss at extinction is nearly independent of pressure, while the peak flame diameter prior to hot-flame extinction decreases with increasing pressure. The maximum hot-flame temperature, inferred from fiber-support radiative emisssions, decreases with increasing pressure, and the hot flames become dimmer with increasing pressure. At 1.0 atm and below there is a prolonged period of coolflame burning that ends with cool-flame extinction at a finite droplet size; the cool-flame-extinction droplet diameter increases and the cool-flame burning rate decreases with decreasing ambient pressure. Above 1.25 atm warm-flame burning and hot-flame re-ignitions become prevalent. At 5.0 atm, there is no abrupt hot-flame extinction with transition to a cool flame; the flame gradually gets dimmer, and the flame temperature decreases over a much longer time, the transition between hot-flame and warm-flame burning becoming almost undiscernible.

Introduction
The first observations of cool flames date back to 1817 (Davy
1817
). Subsequent to the initial discovery of cool flames, cool flame research advanced owing to the importance of low-temperature chemistry in engines, and in particular, engine knock. Advanced engine concepts such as homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) and reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines have the potential for increased efficiency and reduced emissions by increasing operating pressures and lowering operating temperatures; placing more importance on a predictive understanding of low-temperature chemical kinetics. Traditionally most cool-flame research utilized premixed fuel/air mixtures in static (e.g., Mallard and Le Chatelier
1880
) and flow (e.g., Dryer and Glassman
1973
) reactors, rapid compression machines (e.g., Sung and Curran
2014
) and shock tubes (e.g., Hanson and Davidson
2014
; Herbon et al.
2002
). An important concept in cool-flame research is the presence of the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) regime where, at an intermediate temperature range between the cold starting condition and the hot-flame temperature, the overall reactivity (heat release) decreases with increasing temperature.
As highlighted by Law and Faeth (Law and Faeth
1994
), reduced-gravity studies offer geometric simplification (e.g., 1-D flames), and no buoyant flows which allow the study of weak, near-limit flames which include cool flames. Kumagai and Isoda (
1956
) were the first to realize the advantages of the microgravity environment experimentally by studying spherically-symmetric droplet combustion in a one second drop tower at the University of Tokyo. Pearlman and co-workers (Fairlie et al.
2005
; Foster and Pearlman
2006
; Pearlman
2000
), however, were the first to recognize the potential for microgravity studies to provide a window into cool flame research by eliminating the buoyancy-induced flows associated with the low-temperature heat release. The authors used a static reactor and showed how the buoyant flows changes both the flame shape and evolution and cool-flame induction time.
Prior to 2012 most droplet combustion research in microgravity involved the ignition, burning and extinction of ‘hot flames’, with flame temperatures greater than or equal to approximately 1200 K (e.g., Nayagam et al.
1998
). There was a limited amount of research that examined low-temperature chemistry during two-stage ignition of isolated droplets in ambient temperatures below about 900 K (Tanabe et al.
1995
). Studies of large alkane droplets in a long-duration experiment (FlammabilityLimit-Experiment, FLEX) on the International Space Station (ISS) showed, for the first time, quasi-steady droplet combustion sustained by a low temperature or cool flame (Nayagam et al.
2012
; Farouk and Dryer
2014
; Cuoci et al.
2013
). This cool-flame supported droplet burning is possible because of the existence of the NTC regime.
Following the discovery of cool-flame burning in the ISS experiments Ju and coworkers were able to sustain steady cool flames in terrestrial laboratory studies using a counter-flow burner. The initial experiments (Reuter et al.
2016
,
2017a
) used dimethyl ether (DME) and ozone to promote the low-temperature burning. Subsequent experiments, however, used alkane fuels, first with ozone in the oxidizer stream and finally with no ozone (Reuter et al.
2017b
) to produce a cool diffusion flame. Unlike the ISS experiments that have limited resources (i.e., test points and test time), these terrestrial counter-flow experiments provided a detailed flammability map for cool flames across a wide range of fuels and ambient conditions (Reuter et al.
2017b
). These observations of stable cool diffusion flames have given researchers a wealth of insights into cool flame behavior and led to an improved predictive capability of cool-flame behavior; these insights compiled and summarized in recent review articles (Ju
2021
; Ju et al.
2019
).
Cool-flame droplet burning in the FLEX experiments occurred when the hot-flame (ignited by a heated wire) surrounding a large alkane fuel droplet extinguished when the radiative loss from the flame reduced the temperature below that required to sustain combustion (e.g., Dietrich et al.
2014
; Nayagam et al.
1998
; Marchese et al.
1999
). This hot-flame extinction then led to a prolonged period of quasi-steady low-temperature burning characterized by a linear d-squared (droplet-diameter-time) regression and a near-constant flame-standoff ratio (Farouk and Dryer
2014
; Nayagam et al.
2016
). Subsequent FLEX experiments showed that the hot flame is not strictly necessary to achieve cool-flame burning; the cool flame ignition can occur by raising the flash point of the fuel using a much lower ignition energy so as to not overheat the liquid and produce a significant diffusive fuel vapor/air layer around the droplet (Farouk et al.
2017
). The FLEX experiments further showed that the cool flame burns only a fraction of the vaporized fuel, and the unburned fuel re-condenses far outside the flame zone to form a large vapor cloud that is visible on both a backlit view of the droplet and a color camera view of the experiment (Dietrich et al.
2017a
,
b
). When the droplet becomes small enough, the cool flame extinguishes, a process that is characterized by a plateau in the droplet regression history and rapid condensation of the remaining fuel vapor (Nayagam et al.
2015
).
The FLEX experiments also showed the significant influence of pressure on cool-flame droplet burning. The first experiments at hyperbaric pressures and related numerical modeling showed that, in carbon-dioxide-diluted atmospheres, the cool flame could spontaneously re-ignite a hot flame that would subsequently extinguish and initiate further cool-flame burning, a process that could repeat itself multiple times (Farouk et al.
2015
). Subsequent experiments and numerical modeling showed that this process can occur at lower pressures and does not require ambient carbon dioxide (Dietrich et al.
2017a
,
b
; Farouk and Dryer
2022
). Further FLEX experiments and companion modeling (Farouk et al.
2019
) with n-heptane fuel droplets at elevated (3 atm) pressure in helium-diluted ambient environments found that following hot-flame extinction the flame transitions to a ‘warm-flame’ burning mode where the flame temperature is around 970 K for a short period, and then moves into a ‘cool-flame’ mode with a lower flame temperature (∼ 765 K). Independently Ju and co-workers (Yehia et al.
2018
,
2019
) also showed the existence of warm diffusion flames on experiments with their counter-flow burner.
This article presents experimental results of the Cool-Flames-Investigation (CFI) experiments aboard the ISS that studied the low-temperature droplet burning in more detail. The experiments used a new camera system to visualize the cool flame, a variable-gain radiometer, and different fuels and fuel mixtures. The test conditions focused on oxygen/nitrogen mixtures over a range of pressures, including a limited number of tests at the same oxygen index but with helium replacing some of the inert (nitrogen). The present paper summarizes all of the experimental results for n-dodecane in oxygen/nitrogen ambients. Farouk and Dryer (
2022
) presented some of the data earlier in numerical modeling and analyses of hot- and cool-flame burning and extinction phenomena; this work emphasizes the experimental observations and includes radiometer and sooting data not yet available in the literature.
Experimental Apparatus and Data Analysis
The experiments used the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) that is an insert to the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), a full-sized rack inside the Destiny module of the ISS. The hardware and software are identical to that in previous publications (Dietrich et al.
2014
,
2015a
,
b
), except for some important differences. The field-of-view (FOV) of the backlit images of the droplet was increased to approximately 5 cm × 5 cm but used the same image array (1024 × 1024 pixels). This resulted in slightly less spatial resolution but increased the likelihood that a free-floating droplet would stay in the FOV. The recent experiments also used a new intensified camera (12-bit, 1392 × 1040 monochrome pixel array) equipped with a filter wheel and an increased FOV (90 mm × 68 mm). For the hot-flame burning period a filter wheel rotates to place a narrowband 430 nm filter in front of the camera and lens to visualize the
CH
∗
chemiluminescence. When the radiometer detects hot-flame extinction, the filter wheel rotates to put a wideband (390–490 nm) filter in front of the camera so that it can detect the formaldehyde chemiluminescence from the cool flame.
There was a protection system for the camera that shut down the intensifier when the camera and radiometer detected a hot-flame re-ignition during cool-flame burning. This system worked quite well at lower pressures. At higher ambient pressures, however, it became more complex as the hot flames became dimmer, the warm flames brighter and re-ignitions were frequent and unpredictable. As a result there were periods of the test where there was no image data from the intensified camera because either the wrong filter was in place and/or the camera shut down because of a hot-flame re-ignition.
The droplets in the previous FLEX experiments were primarily free-floated in the chamber. Some experiments, however, ‘tethered’ the droplet to an 80 µm silicon-carbide (SiC) fiber to maintain all of the events within the FOV of all of the cameras. This tethering significantly increased the likelihood of a successful test, but led to perturbations in the burning process, especially at small droplet diameters, such as near cool-flame extinction. To further reduce perturbations to the burning process, the present experiments used a smaller 40 µm carbide fiber to tether the droplet.
To improve flame radiation observations, the fixed-gain amplification used in the prior FLEX experiments was replaced by a variable-gain amplifier to better resolve the flame radiance during both the hot-flame and cool-flame burning periods. This modification was especially important for recording the narrowband radiometer observations (looking at water vapor emission in the 5–7 µm range) at both cool- and hot-flame burning conditions without saturating the amplifier.
Finally, software modifications were implemented to better control the energy supplied to the droplet during the ignition phase of each experiment. Whereas the previous ISS droplet-combustion experiments used a preset ignition time, the current experiments used feedback from the radiometers to determine when ignition of the developing fuel vapor/oxidizer layer occurred. Once the radiometer detected flame initiation, the control computer turned off the igniters and retracted them from the droplet automatically. The radiometer values chosen to indicate ignition and extinction of the hot flame were set by the test operators prior to each experiment and could be changed from test to test.
The fuel for the results presented in this article was pure n-dodecane and the ambient gas mixtures were oxygen/nitrogen (0.21/0.79 and 0.17/0.83
O
2
/N
2
mole fraction). The ambient pressure ranged from 0.50 to 5.0 atm; the higher pressures representing a change from the previous FLEX experiments that were limited to 3.0 atm. In theory the experiments could have used droplet diameters from approximately 1 mm to over 7 mm based on previous ISS droplet combustion experiments. Droplets smaller than 3–3.5 mm tend to burn to completion and do not exhibit radiative hot-flame extinction and cool-flame burning. Larger droplets, however, use large amounts of fuel and have very long test times (thus consuming large amounts of digital storage and requiring long downlink times). As a result, with a few exceptions, all of the tests used initial droplet sizes in the 4–5 mm range.
The cool flames from the ISS droplet combustion experiments are very dim, invisible to the color video camera on the MDCA and barely discernible with the intensified camera. The images improve with median filtering and image-averaging over 500 ms (Nayagam et al.
2016
). Automated image-processing procedures provide a measure of the flame diameter from a line profile across the center of the flame. Reported here are two relevant measures of the cool flame, the peak-to-peak flame diameter representing the diameter of peak chemiluminescence and a full-width, half-max (FWHM) diameter that represents the outer diameter of the flame where the grayscale value of the flame chemiluminescence reaches one half the peak value.
Model Descriptions
Numerical Model
The mathematical model employed to describe the transient vaporization, flame initiation, and combustion histories of isolated pure and multi-component fuel droplets in the high-, intermediate-, and low-temperature regimes under microgravity conditions uses the numerical model described in detail in previous works (Alam et al.
2019
; Farouk et al.
2021
; Farouk and Dryer
2014
). The model solves the conservation equations for mass, species, and energy for both the liquid and gas phases assuming spherical symmetry. It includes both Fickian and Soret diffusion for evaluating multicomponent species diffusion velocities in the gas phase. A statistical narrow-band radiation model is employed to obtain spectral radiative effects. The model is also capable of resolving the thermal perturbation resulting from tethering fibers (Farouk and Dryer
2011
). Liquid-phase property data are taken from the Daubert and Danner database (Daubert and Danner
1989
). A comprehensive detailed kinetic model consisting of 583 species and 2609 reactions (Sarathy et al.
2011
) describes the gas-phase chemical reactions of n-dodecane and is a construct developed for n-alkanes covering a carbon number range from
C
7
-
C
20
. The mechanism resolves the high, intermediate and low-temperature kinetic regimes for n-dodecane. The far field is typically two hundred times the initial droplet diameter with Dirichlet boundary conditions for fixed ambient composition and temperature. The numerical model formulation does not include consideration of soot formation.
The spatial discretization is a node-centered finite-volume scheme with second-order accuracy. Time discretization is a backward-difference formula, up to fifth order, with a variable time step, making it a fully implicit multipoint interpolation scheme. The complete set of coupled partial differential and algebraic equations are discretized first in space and then integrated in time in an automated fashion as a set of coupled ordinary differential–algebraic equations. This approach is appropriate for the large range of time scales and stability constraints imposed by the current chemically reacting system. The numerical scheme can resolve the flame dynamics associated with ignition and extinction as well as re-ignition efficiently without compromising computation time.

Immediately after hot-flame extinction the soot shell surrounding the droplet begins to expand rapidly away from the droplet. The rapid expansion is likely the result of the imbalance between the Stefan drag that remains nearly unchanged (as a result of the nearly identical burning-rate constant for cool and hot flames) and the thermophoretic force on the soot that decreases considerably after the hot flame extinguishes. This condensed-fuel vapor cloud attenuates the background illumination of the droplet.

The predicted time of ∼ 13 s at which the transition from hot-flame to cool-flame burning takes place agrees very well with the experiments. The flame radiance decreases by a factor of approximately 5 when the hot-to-cool flame transition occurs. The model predicts a maximum temperature of approximately 780
K

) fuels. In agreement with the experiment, the model shows that during the cool-flame burn the flame diameter is a factor of approximately 4 lower than that of the hot flame. Despite the much lower flame temperature, the predicted droplet regression rate remains nearly unchanged. Dodecane has a high flash point temperature, specific heat and latent heat of vaporization (344 K, 376 kJ/kmol K, and 61.40 kJ/mol) and therefore requires higher energy input to achieve a flammable vapor/air envelope around the droplet. The higher specific heat and latent heat of vaporization results in slower burning early in the hot-flame period. The slow response, however, is only present during the evolution to high-temperature combustion. The model predicts a prolonged cool-flame burn, with a duration of approximately 32 s, after which all burning extinguishes. The predicted cool-flame extinction diameter of 0.14 mm is smaller than that measured in the experiment.

Cool- and Warm-Flame Burning Rates
The average burning-rate constants during the hot- and cool-flame burning periods are easily measured from the data in Fig.
1
; the burning rate for the cool flame is a linear diameter-square fit of the droplet history from the time shortly after hot-flame extinction to shortly before cool-flame extinction. For ambient pressures less than 2 atm this is a straight-forward process. For ambient pressures of 2 atm and above, however, the hot flame will periodically re-ignite and extinguish during the cool-flame burning period. For these tests, the burning rate is obtained from the initial portion of the cool-flame burning period before the re-ignitions start. Figure

The results show that the cool-flame burning-rate constant increases continuously from the lowest pressure tested (0.50 atm) to approximately 3 atm. The limited data from 3 - 5 atm suggest that the burning-rate constant is relatively constant. Above 2 atm, however, it may not be appropriate to call it the cool-flame burning-rate constant as in this region the droplet burns in the warm-flame regime which is characterized by flames that are closer in size to the hot flame, with flame radiances (broadband) that are also closer to those of the hot-flame radiance. In addition, the hot-flame re-ignitions from the cool/warm flames frequently occur at ambient pressures of 2 atm and above. The burning-rate constants in Fig.
4
are from the post-hot-flame period before any re-ignition.
The numerical simulations show that for pressures higher than 2.5 atm the flame, after the radiative extinction of the hot flame, transitions to a quasi-steady warm flame and burns to completion. The predicted average burning rate in the 2.5 - 5.0 atm pressure range represents the warm-flame burn as no cool-flame burning takes place in this pressure range. The predicted average burning rate as a function of pressure over the entire range is highly nonlinear and clearly shows the presence of the two apparently distinct regimes. These two regimes are characterized by the two different slopes, although the data are not extensive enough to verify that, given the experimental uncertainties producing scatter. In the pressure range of 0.50 - 1.25 atm the average burning rate increases sharply as a function of pressure; this is the cool-flame burning regime. As the pressure increases to 2.0 atm and higher the droplet burns in the warm-flame regime. The average burning rate in the warm-flame regime is higher than that of the cool-flame regime but is less sensitive to pressure, which is apparent in a relatively weaker slope of burning rate as a function of pressure in the 2 - 5 atm range. The cool-flame analytical predictions, although closer to the data than the numerical results in an overall sense, exhibit a noticeably smaller slope than the numerical and experimental results, suggesting the need for further attention to predicted pressure dependence in future analytical studies.
Cool-Flame Extinction Diameters
At ambient pressures less than or equal to 1.25 atm, the cool-flame burning period ended when the cool flame extinguished at a finite droplet size. Cool-flame extinction is evidenced by a distinct plateau in the droplet history that is coincident with the time at which the cool flame disappears from the intensified camera (Fig.
1
). There is also a change in flame radiance when the cool flame extinguishes, although this inflection point in the radiance is not as pronounced for n-dodecane as it is for n-heptane.

This is due to the fact that it competes with production of the ketohydroperoxide, as heat losses push the maximum reaction temperature in the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) regime toward the turnover temperature. As the pressure increases beyond 1.5 atm, no cool-flame extinction is observed in the simulations (or the experiments), despite hot-cool or hot-warm flame-transition having occurred.
For pressures 2.5 atm and higher, a cool-flame burn is completely absent, and the droplet transitions to a warm flame from the hot flame, burning to completion. Besides some experimental departures from spherical symmetry, differences from numerical predictions may be due to uncertainties in low-temperature kinetics, while there are differences from analytical predictions that are caused by omission of warm-flame steps that become increasingly important with increasing pressure.
Flame Diameter and Luminosity
Immediately after ignition, the flames are small and very luminous, the visible image being dominated by broadband visible radiation, presumably from soot. The flames then grow and the luminosity from soot decreases rapidly. The flame continues to grow, with soot luminosity disappearing and with the remaining blue flame getting progressively dimmer. Near radiative extinction, the flame is near its peak size and is dim-blue in all of the experiments, regardless of pressure (Fig.
2
e–i). Figure
6

Sooting Behavior
The CFI tests also reveal the significant influence of ambient pressure on the sooting behavior of both the cool and hot flames. Figure
10
shows the backlit view of the droplet at the mid-points of both the hot-flame and cool-flame burning periods for the range of pressures tested. Following ignition there is a pronounced soot shell that forms around the droplet at ambient pressures less than or equal to 2 atm. This soot shell gets more dense and moves closer to the droplet as the ambient pressure increases. At the two pressures tested above 2 atm the soot shell becomes more of a cloud that surrounds the droplet and nearly obscures the droplet surface in the backlit images.
Fig. 10

The soot shell forms because of the balance of the Stefan drag force pushing the soot away from the droplet and the thermophoretic force on the soot particles that pulls the soot towards the droplet. At low pressures, following hot-flame extinction, the soot shell gets pushed away from the droplet into the quiescent ambient atmosphere because the thermophoretic force essentially disappears with the hot flame. As pressure increases, the drag force decreases because the magnitude of the Stefan-flow velocity decreases. In addition, the warm flame may introduce a thermophoretic force (owing to its increased temperature and larger diameter) on the soot that increases with pressure, resulting in a soot cloud that can remain close to the droplet at higher pressures.
The backlit images near hot-flame extinction (e.g., Fig.
2
d) suggest little formation of soot after that formed immediately after ignition. In addition, the color camera images show luminous radiation from soot to be completely absent at hot-flame radiative extinction (the flames are entirely blue). Neglecting soot formation during the hot-flame burning period is therefore a reasonable assumption in the numerical model. For cool-flame burning less than 2 atm pressure there is no soot in the vicinity of the droplet (Fig.
10
) as it gets pushed away from the droplet by the initial hot flame and subsequent cool flame Stefan flow. Therefore neglecting soot formation during cool-flame burning at 2 atm pressure and below is also a reasonable assumption. At higher pressures, however, the cool/warm-flame burning is more complex, and sooting may be present and how it impacts burning is more uncertain.
Discussion
This data documents the significant influence of the ambient pressure on the low-temperature-burning regime of n-dodecane droplets. At pressures less than or equal to one
atm
, in the experiments there is a prolonged period of cool-flame burning following radiative extinction of the hot flame that ends when the cool flame extinguishes at a finite droplet extinction diameter. This droplet diameter increases with decreasing ambient pressure. This process is currently understood by both numerical (e.g., Farouk and Dryer
2022
) and analytical (e.g., Nayagam et al.
2015
) treatments of the droplet combustion problem.
At pressures greater than 1.25 atm, the droplet burning after hot-flame extinction becomes more complex as hot-flame re-ignitions and warm-flame burning can all occur, and the behavior is less predictable. One particularly noteworthy aspect is the transition from a hot flame to a cool/warm flame at high pressures. Figure
11
shows the importance of ambient pressure on this transition with tests at 0.50 and 5.0 atm plotted. The CIR had another black-and-white camera that had a near-infrared filter to visualize the luminescence of the fiber during fiber-supported tests. Previous FLEX experiments (Dietrich et al.
2015a
,
b
) used this camera to obtain peak gas-phase temperatures for fiber-supported decane/hexanol droplets. The present experiments used a different filter that allowed detection of lower-temperature flames, but this also meant the ground calibration from the previous FLEX tests was no longer valid so data are presented here only on camera grayscale and not absolute temperature. Figure
11
also compares numerical simulations of both the FLEX-1238 and FLEX-1260 tests to the experimental data.

Figure

shows the total peak fiber luminescence, flame diameter (using the distance between the peaks of where the flame impinges on the fiber) and total flame radiance as functions of time for the droplets at two different pressures. Consistent with the data in Fig.
6
, the graph shows that the hot-flame diameter is significantly smaller at 5.0 atm than at 0.50 atm. At 0.50 atm the flame radiance rises quickly and reaches peak value near 25 W, and it remains near that value until hot-flame extinction, after which it quickly drops to a value less that 5 W during cool-flame burning.
The experiment and numerical prediction clearly show the hot-flame-to-cool-flame transition for the 0.50 atm test. The peak hot-flame radiance is predicted to be approximately 30 W, higher than the measured value. The predicted flame-diameter temporal evolution follows the experimental trajectory reasonably well, with the transition to cool-flame burning taking place at approximately 15 s, about 4 s later than the measured value. During the quasi-steady cool-flame burning the model predicts a flame radiance of approximately 3 W, which agrees favorably with the measurements. During low-temperature burning the flame maintains a flame diameter of approximately 10 mm. The flame-temperature evolution shows that during the early stage of high-temperature burning the temperature decreases sharply and then approaches a quasi-steady condition prior to the transition to cool-flame burning. The model predicts a peak hot-flame temperature of approximately 1170 K just prior to the transition to cool-flame burning and a nearly constant peak temperature of approximately 740 K during cool-flame burning.
The test at 5.0 atm is completely different. The flame-diameter, flame-radiance and peak-fiber-grayscale data show no clear transition between hot-flame burning and warm-flame burning. The peak fiber grayscale is saturated initially and shows a continuous decrease after ignition, with some small hot-flame re-ignitions before it reaches a steady value (constant peak flame temperature) during warm-flame burning. The flame-diameter and flame-radiance data also show a smooth transition, with some perturbations associated with minor hot-flame re-ignitions. Previous FLEX testing showed that as pressure increases the hot flames get progressively dimmer (Dietrich et al.
2017a
,
b
). This was also true in the CFI dodecane tests presented here. At the lower pressures, the hot flames viewed with the intensified camera and color camera were relatively easy to track and identify. At higher pressures, however, the hot flames became almost invisible in both cameras.
Unlike the experiments, the simulation clearly shows a transition in the flame radiance and flame diameter evolution between hot- and warm-flame burning. In the first stage the model predicts a maximum hot-flame radiance of approximately 40 W, which then reduces to approximately 18 W in the second, warm-flame stage. The flame diameter reaches a peak value of about 25 mm and then reduces to around 19 mm as the system proceeds to warm-flame burning. The variation in both the flame radiance and flame diameter between the transitions is much smaller at 5.0 atm than it is at 0.50 atm. The temperature predictions clearly show that at 5.0 atm pressure the temporal change of the peak flame temperature is slower than at 0.50 atm, but a quasi-steady hot flame is never achieved. It is interesting to note that the transition from the hot to warm flame at 5.0 atm occurs at approximately 1096 K which is similar to the value predicted for 0.50 atm. In comparison to the 0.50 atm case, where the transition from hot- to cool-flame burning happens abruptly, the hot- to warm-flame transition occurs relatively slowly at 5.0 atm. The change in the temperature during the hot- to warm-flame transition is also small at 5.0 atm, with a quasi-steady warm-flame temperature of about 1000 K. The smaller nature of the change may be one of the reasons that the differences between the experiments and predictions are not discernible.
Kinetically, an increase in the operating pressure results in an increase in both the turnover temperature into the NTC regime and hot ignition-temperature transition associated with hydrogen-peroxide decomposition, at the terminus of the NTC temperature regime. The difference in the reactivity between the two temperatures, however, decreases with increasing pressure. The warm flame is dictated by the NTC kinetics and a competition for
OH
between the hydrocarbon and oxygenated hydrocarbon fragments. The oxidation of
CO

CO

CO

CO

CO

. Since the flame radius during warm-flame burning is much larger than that during cool-flame burning (e.g., Fig.

) and the flame temperatures are higher, radiative losses become more significant during warm-flame burning. The radiative heat loss decreases the flame temperature, but the diffusive losses of species are insufficient to slow down the NTC reactions that define the heat-generation time scale. As a result, the peak temperature in the warm flame initially decreases from about 1050 K to 990 K and then increases back to about 1055 K. Despite the variation in the flame temperature, the warm-flame burning rate continually decreases, albeit slowly.
Conclusions
This paper presented comprehensive data from large, isolated n-dodecane droplet combustion experiments in microgravity conducted aboard the ISS. The experiments were primarily in air (with a few tests at reduced oxygen) and ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. The experiments show the significant impact of pressure on cool- and warm-flame burning with cool-flame burning and extinction observed at lower pressures following hot-flame radiative extinction. At higher pressures warm-flame burning and hot-flame re-ignition became more prevalent. The experimental observations were quantified by measurements of the droplet burning rate, extinction droplet diameters, flame diameters and flame radiative energy loss.
Detailed numerical modeling shows good agreement with the experiments particularly at lower pressures. The (small) disagreement between the model and experiments at these pressures is likely the result of experimental uncertainties, inaccuracies in the low and intermediate temperature chemistry models and physical effects, such as fuel (and large fuel fragments) vapor condensation (Williams et al.
2021
), not included in the model formulation. At higher pressures the experiments became less repeatable with spontaneous hot-flame re-ignitions that made measurements of droplet burning rate, flame size and radiative energy loss more difficult. Despite the lack of a large data set at higher pressures (large number of tests to develop statistical confidence and error bands) the model still does a reasonable job in predicting both qualitatively and quantitatively the experimental observations.
The data from the CFI experiments are beneficial in the development and validation of numerical models of low and intermediate chemistry in a more realistic (diffusive, two-phase system), but geometrically simple (spherically symmetric) combustion system. The CFI experiments also included tests (not reported in this paper) that examined how fuel structure influenced cool- and warm-flame burning. These tests involved dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures as well as tests with farnesane (a sustainable aviation fuel) and the data is publicly available (psi.ndc.nasa.gov) and will be the subject of subsequent publications by the authors. Future experiments that have more detailed diagnostics would enable a more detailed comparison between model predictions.
